title: Demond Claiborne's Vikings Future Could Be Crystal Clear After Week 7
full_text:
There's no sugarcoating it: Vikings rookie running back Demond Claiborne has been a huge letdown early in the 2026 NFL season . The preseason hype built around his excellent training camp, where he showed great speed and athleticism, has not translated into regular-season success.
Claiborne played in four of the Vikings' first five games, but the rookie running back has only six rushing attempts for 13 yards and two catches for eight receiving yards. He has played 18 offensive snaps for the Purple and Gold this season despite Jordan Mason being on injured reserve and Aaron Jones Sr. playing through a knee injury , further hammering home that the Vikings don't trust the first-year runner.
If head coach Kevin O'Connell trusted Minnesota's sixth-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft more, he would receive more opportunities. Instead, the 23-year-old rookie is finding himself on the sidelines instead of on the field, and it might not be much longer before his future with the Vikings becomes crystal clear.
After sitting out Week 1 against the Green Bay Packers, Claiborne has struggled to get playing time. He hasn't played double-digit snaps in a game yet, but came close in Week 4 against the Miami Dolphins when he played nine snaps.
Demond Claiborne offensive snaps
That said, Mason—who had 15 carries in Week 1—is expected to return from injured reserve now that his thumb has healed, which means Claiborne could be used even less moving forward. Even then, the rookie will still be splitting RB3 work with DeeJay Dallas, making those opportunities even more scarce.
Dallas's seven years of experience have led to him having a bigger offensive role than Claiborne this season. He also knows general manager Nolan Teasley from their days in Seattle. The veteran running back has played 40 offensive snaps this year, carrying the ball three times for 10 yards and catching four passes for 34 yards.
At this point, it seems unnecessary to keep Claiborne on the 53-man roster for any reason other than the fear of another team claiming him off waivers or signing him off the practice squad. It might be too early for Minnesota to give up on him or risk losing him, so it is understandable not to gamble with his future.
The most logical move for the Vikings moving forward might be to keep Claiborne inactive on game day until there is a role for him on offense. Keeping him dressed and active when he isn't contributing as a running back and has played only four special teams snaps doesn't make sense.
Keep a close eye on Claiborne's role in Week 7 against the Indianapolis Colts . If he doesn't get involved on the field or blows any limited chances he gets, expect the Vikings to change how they'll handle the rookie's development moving forward.

title: Vikings' Biggest Need Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline Is Painfully Obvious
full_text:
The undefeated Vikings need to decide how aggressive they will be before the 2026 NFL trade deadline , which takes place on Tuesday, Nov. 10. If the Purple and Gold feel they are truly contenders, general manager Nolan Teasley should do what he can to strengthen the roster and prepare for a potential playoff run.
The Vikings have been fortunate to lean on defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit and the strong leg of kicker Will Reichard through the first five games of the season, but teams will soon start exploiting any weaknesses Minnesota's roster could have.
Much of the trade talk around the Purple and Gold involves offensive players ,  as Vikings fans want to see the team trade for a weapon to help put points on the board. That said, the team's biggest weakness is actually a defensive position that desperately needs more depth.
The strong play of other defenders, particularly close to the line of scrimmage, has hidden the Vikings' struggles at safety fairly well. At one time, the combination of Harrison Smith and Josh Metellus was enough to carry the position, but that duo has struggled to be effective this year .
Smith is 37 years old and in his ninth season as a pro. For the first time in his career, he is playing less than half of Minnesota's defensive snaps. Even in his limited role, he has been the worst safety in the league , earning a 31.5 Pro Football Focus grade—dead last among 98 qualified players.
Metellus isn't much better than Smith when it comes to PFF . The 28-year-old defensive back's 40.2 grade ranks him 93rd while allowing a 145.8 passer rating to opposing quarterbacks.
Even Theo Jackson (63.7 PFF grade) and Jay Ward (59.9 PFF grade) have been just okay. However, Ward has only played two defensive snaps, while Jackson has been attempting to pick up the slack with 191 defensive snaps.
The Vikings have rookies Jacob Thomas and Jakobe Thomas on the roster to insert into the lineup when they are ready, but Minnesota needs to do something to get better play at the safety position this year.
Don't be surprised if the Purple and Gold explore trade options before the Nov. 10 deadline. To keep the defense strong for the rest of the season, adding an experienced safety to Flores's aggressive unit would prove that the Vikings are serious about being contenders this season.

The New England Patriots ' three game-winning streak was snapped on Thursday night, as they lost to the Chicago Bears 30-24 at Soldier Field . It was a weird game, as the Patriots played well enough to find ways to find the game. But ultimately, they struggled on both sides of the ball to make the one extra winning play.
"It's a thin margin when you play good teams," Mike Vrabel said postgame. "We did some good things. But again, didn't do enough. We didn't get enough stops in the red zone and we didn't convert our red zone opportunity the one time, so. That's probably the difference in the game."

title: An Oral History Of Patriots WR Kyle Dixon's 'Twisted' Collegiate Baseball Career
full_text:
Kyle Dixon , the 26-year-old wide receiver from Carlinville, Illinois, was a multi-sport athlete in high school. He was a fantastic wide receiver, a fantastic defensive back and an even better pitcher.
His journey out of Carlinville High School started on the mound. It's now taken him onto the sidelines for the New England Patriots .
How in the world did that happen?
When you ask Dixon — now on the Patriots practice squad — he still doesn't really know. He can try to explain his winding road to the NFL, but there's so many stops along the way that sometimes he forgets a few things. So here's everyone else he's crossed paths with to help fill in the puzzle.
Kyle, born in 2001 to Tim and Monica Dixon, played baseball, football and wrestled in high school. He was excellent in everything he did. His coaches rave about his athletic abilities, almost to a fault.
Don Borgini, former Carlinville baseball head coach: "He was a fierce competitor."
Monica Dixon, Kyle's mother: "He excelled in all of his sports, but was looking for ways to improve his skills. He was always looking online for new training techniques."
Kyle Dixon: "Baseball was a little bit more special for me."
Maybe it was just the athletic juices in his veins, but Kyle always lived for the moment. The homemade pitchers mound that Kyle and his grandfather made in his backyard certainly helped. Once high school rolled around, baseball is where he found his groove.
Borgini: "Every coach on Earth wants a kid that wants the ball in the moment, and Kyle is certainly that guy."
Monica Dixon: "When he did get to pitch, I had a lot of anxiety. His dad could always handle that pressure better than me."
Kyle Dixon: "It was something I really enjoyed a lot."
Borgini: "In a sectional game, he had 19 strikeouts of the 21 batters and it was a tremendous performance by him that I won't forget. ... It is the top (game) for me as far as a pitcher goes (that I've ever seen)."
Kyle Dixon: "It might have been the last game I ever played (in high school). ... We ended up losing that game."
Borgini: "He was attracting a lot of attention."
Monica Dixon: "As parents, it was nice to see his hard work pay off when he got his scholarship. He earned it."
Kyle officially committed to Southern Illinois after a coach at a local JUCO help connect the two parties. But he had committed when Ken Henderson was the head coach. Henderson was fired and the abrupt change caught Kyle — who was on his way to vacation — off guard. Still, from the first day on campus, he stood out.
Lance Rhodes, Southern Illinois baseball head coach: "He wasn't the typical high school-sized kid that was coming to college. He was very put together, just a good looking kid. He definitely looked the part."
Kyle Dixon: "You don't really know what to expect as a freshman, especially with the new staff that didn't recruit you. It was an interesting start to college."
Rhodes: "He (was) just as big as the seniors. He had a ton of ability and he threw extremely hard."
Kyle Dixon: "I was off to a pretty good start my freshman year and then we stopped. We couldn't go into our facility to train with it being COVID. We couldn't go to a lot of the gyms or anything to work out."
His freshman year was mangled by the pandemic, where he only played in eight games. He pitched in four more as a sophomore, but a 22.50 earned run average plagued him. It was a pair of trying years for Dixon. He watched pro pitchers like Max Scherzer and Aroldis Chapman to try and figure out his form.
Kyle Dixon: "I became very focused on looking at MLB pitchers' mechanics and then trying to figure out how I wanted mine to look in regards to that. ... I think I became too focused on mechanics."
Monica Dixon: "I think he started putting more pressure on himself to be perfect and it just wasn't happening. As a parent, it was hard to watch."
Rhodes: "Kyle was always one of those guys that the feel of pitching was something that he needed to develop and work on, and I really think the COVID break in action ... was probably the toughest thing for him."
Kyle Dixon: "I kept thinking if I just keep figuring out whatever mechanical thing it is, then it's gonna play, then it's gonna click. The reality, that was the problem in and of itself."
He didn't want to stick around. After his scholarship was pulled, Southern Illinois Edwardsville — who did research on him coming out of high school — came calling.
Sean Lyons, SIUE baseball head coach: "I had a local umpire stop by our baseball office, come in and tell our staff there's this really good arm pitching, high school kid, not too far from here. ... When Kyle decided to transfer from (Southern Illinois) Carbondale, we kind of had a connection."
Monica Dixon: "We just went with the flow. He would always talk to us about moving and the reasoning for it."
Kyle Dixon: "Ironically, the pitching coach there was the one who recruited me to Carbondale. I was really comfortable with him."
But that coach would later take the head coaching gig for SIUE's softball program, and so Dixon was left with another surprising staff change. Still, his stuff on the mound never left.
Lyons: "He could throw the baseball in the lower-to-mid 90s. Sometimes command and where the location of that was sometimes a mystery for him. But when it was right, man, it was really good."
Kyle Dixon: "I wouldn't say I had a good year, but it was a better year. It wasn't good, but it was progress compared to the year before."
Lyons: "He had a skillset on the mound that could have possibly given him the option ... to play professionally as a baseball player."
Kyle Dixon: "Without a doubt."
Maybe it was time to get out of Illinois. Kyle called Lyons to let him know that he would be entering the transfer portal, a decision that he think took his coach by surprise. After having some summer league teammates hype up Georgia Gwinnett, Kyle then made the trip down south to a team that would go on to make eight-straight NAIA World Series appearances, a streak still active.
Jeremy Sheetinger, former Georgia Gwinnett baseball head coach: "When you see a kid that looks like Kyle and he's built like an Adonis, you know that there's something in there. ... We just feel like sometimes Division I schools, if a kid doesn't gave it, they get pushed to the side. We could spent a little bit more time with them."
Braxton Meguiar, former Georgia Gwinnett second baseman (who played baseball with Mike Vrabel's son, Carter, at Wabash Valley Community College in 2021): "I always remember Kyle's work ethic being different. He never changed. He never wavered, even when he wasn't having success."
Like the previous two schools, it just wasn't in the cards. Kyle had the yips, most commonly associated when throwing a baseball accurately becomes a chore. He'd walk away from sports entirely at the end of the season.
Kyle Dixon: "I was still kind of holding out optimism that I was going to be able to figure it out and turn it around."
Sheetinger: "He was good for a hit an inning, a strikeout an inning and a walk an inning. ... Kyle didn't make our postseason roster."
Meguiar: "He was having some control problems."
Sheetinger: "He's a guy that didn't impact us on the field, but he impacted with the kind of kid he was."
Kyle Dixon: "I just tried to be as good as a teammate as I could and really just not let what was happening to me affect my teammates. It's never fair to them. I think I was partially being myself and then having a little awareness about how not to act."
Monica Dixon: "We were sad for him. His love for the sport had faded. He was done completely."
Sheetinger: "Our pitchers threw footballs. But more people started watching the way Kyle would go catch footballs. You could see it coming together."
Baseball was in the rearview window. Instead, Kyle moved back home and picked up a job in sales, selling marketing tools for pool companies. All the while, filming workout videos to see what could come of his extra years of…

title: 4 Postive Takeaways From Patriots' Thursday Night Loss to Bears
full_text:
After falling to the Chicago Bears (5-2) on Thursday Night Football, many are quick to pick apart what went wrong for the New England Patriots and what needs to improve. Those conversations are centered around third down defense, tackling, wide receiver play, and other scrutinies from the Patriots 30-24 let down.
However, like most games, the Patriots still put out good tape, despite the outcome. Here's what New England did well on Thursday night and what we learned about this team moving forward:
With a diminished wide receiver room, the Patriots had to rely on other skill position players to push the ball through the passing game. One of the few that stepped up on Thursday was rookie tight end Eli Raridon.
Raridon hauled in 3 catches for 56 yards, including a 30-yard touchdown reception on a seam route in the third quarter. Maye targeted Raridon earlier in the game but was intercepted in the redzone.
Raridon now has more receiving yards (168) and touchdowns (two) this season than Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III, and A.J. Brown. The third-round pick out of Notre Dame has turned out to be a great investment by the Pats, and will carry the team's pass game well after Hunter Henry retires or moves on from New England.
The Patriots are among the top teams in the NFL for players listed as inactive on reserve lists. Entering Thursday night, the Patriots had 22 players on reserve lists, with nine of those players being starters.
Most notably, the Patriots were missing four guards on Thursday, and were forced to start Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor . While the two players struggled, New England's offensive line had a decent performance, only allowing two sacks on quarterback Drake Maye.
Additionally, the Patriots had three inactive cornerbacks on Thursday, including starter Carlton Davis. Christian Gonzalez was also listed as questionable ahead of the game with an illness, but played every defensive snap.
Lastly, the Pats were limited to just four wide receievers, with Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs on the injured reserve.
With Chicago being one of the NFL's top teams, and last year's second ranked NFC team, New England's competitive showing was impressive, considering the diverse roster they were forced to use.
Similar to the last point, injuries have been a major hurdle the Patriots have had to overcome this season. Each game, the Pats leave with more diagnoses than they entered with.
Last night, the Patriots stayed relatively healthy. With depth being an issue, the health of New England's team was crucial to staying in yesterday's game.
The only significant injury was suffered by defensive linemen Christian Barmore, who appeared to sustain an upper-body injury after sacking Caleb Williams late in the game.
With 10 days until they travel to Miami, Patriots players will have plenty of time to recover from past injuries.
Running back Rhamondre Stevenson was one of the best players on the field Thursday night, and was crucial to New England's ability to stay in the game.
The sixth-year player only ran for 22 yards against the Bears defense, but carried the ball six times, which is twice the amount of his counterpart, TreVeyon Henderson.
Most notably, Stevenson impacted the game through his pass-catching. He hauled in 5 receptions for 93 yards and was New England's leading receiver. His 48-yard touchdown reception to end the first half kept the Patriots within scoring distance of the Bears for the rest of the game.
RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️ 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW
This season, Stevenson has 25 more carries than Henderson and has notched 82 more yards than the second-year player. While Henderson has dealt with an ankle injury over the past two weeks, the only action he's missed was Week 1 against Seattle.
Stevenson's production and usage points to continued increase in carries and impact plays from the veteran Patriot.

title: Drake Maye's Interception Wasn't The Reason The Patriots Lost
full_text:
CHICAGO — The New England Patriots didn't win on Thursday Night Football, and yet, their quarterback had yet another great performance.
Drake Maye threw for 300 yards for the second time in three weeks, scored 3+ total touchdowns for the fourth-straight game and used his legs to extend plenty of plays behind a banged-up offensive line.
Did he throw a bad interception in the first half that took points off the board? Yes.
Was that play the biggest reason for the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears ? Nope.
Maye was hard on himself after the game, taking the brunt of the blame for the bad interception he threw to Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson. He was trying to hit Eli Raridon for a touchdown to cut into Chicago's 13-7 lead. Instead, he didn't put enough air on the throw and it was turned over.
“It definitely was a huge point in the game. It’s those plays, I talk about all the time," Maye said. "And those plays that can swing the game, can impact the game, and that was definitely one of them right there. I wish I definitely had that one back and a lot of plays.
"But got to give credit to them. They had a good plan on a short week and they got after us. ...  I know that was a big turning point in the game and I know I let my team down."
But the Patriots had a bigger reason for the loss, and it was from the other side of the ball. The Patriots really couldn't tackle all night, and according to Pro Football Focus, they missed 16 tackles. That's the most they've had in a single game since Super Bowl LX. Marcus Jones led the Patriots with five.
Chicago controlled the ground game with D'Andre Swift (22 carries, 78 yards, 1 rushing touchdown) and beat the Patriots' zone coverages all night.
“The tackling wasn’t good enough, not against this team," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "We knew coming in, certainly against this team, whether it’s Swift, (Luther) Burden, the quarterback. It just leads to extra yards and conversions. But, we fought. I would say that we need to turn the ball over and tackle better and those are fundamental skills."
Caleb Williams hit eight passes for 20+ yards, really stressing the secondary that was down three cornerbacks coming into the game.
Ultimately, the Patriots lost the game, not because of Maye's play, but because of everything around it. There wasn't a lot of production from the ground game or the wide receivers, penalties ran rampant and the defense struggled to bring anyone down.
And yet, Maye kept them in it. He shouldn't be the one receiving the pointed finger.
"He gave us a chance. He competed and I know he’d like to have that throw back to Eli but, I thought he really competed," Vrabel said. "Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football. He gave us a chance. I know he’d like to have that one back and he’ll learn from it like he always does. I’m glad he’s ours."

title: Patriots' Rhamondre Stevenson Details 'Momentum' Last-Second TD Scamper
full_text:
CHICAGO — The Chicago Bears had just scored, with Luther Burden weaving his way into the end zone. They were up 20-7 over the New England Patriots and looked like they might run away with the game at halftime.
And yet, in a blink of an eye, the Patriots stormed into the locker room trailing by just one possession.
After hitting A.J. Brown on an 18-yard in cut, the Patriots quickly called a timeout with three seconds left. Then, lining up in a Hail Mary-like formation (three receivers spread out wide to one side), Drake Maye checked it down to Rhamondre Stevenson out of the backfield.
Brown came across the field to help clear out room for Stevenson, who'd use a big block from DeMario Douglas to pick up what turned into a 48-yard touchdown run to close the first half.
RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️ 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW
It was a play that's been in the Patriots' back pocket for the last few seasons.
"I was just trying to make a play, put my team in a position to swing the game a little bit as much as we can," Stevenson said after the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Bears on Thursday Night Football .
"We've been working on that play for a long time and came in handy today. Executed on that play, so felt good to do that."
What was Stevenson's mindset during the play?
"Score. Score," he said. "I felt like it brought us some momentum. Felt like it brought us some momentum, but obviously, not enough, you know? We didn't come out with the win."
That play was part of Stevenson's career-high 93 yards through the air, the most on the team. The running game wasn't really working for the Patriots all night, but Stevenson was able to impact the game through the air.
"Just trying to give us a chance to go down and run. And I think it’s hard when those things, I kind of had a feeling they were going to come after me and blitz," Maye said on the play. "So when it leaves, we get five out in the pattern and they bring five. We got really five, four blockers, and Mondre with the ball, and they got six defenders, and it all takes one cut. So that was pretty cool. How you draw it up. That’s how we drew it up all. We’ve been practicing that play since OTAs. So, it definitely brought us some life at halftime, and then just didn’t really swing for us in the fourth quarter."
As a runner, Stevenson carried the ball six times for 22 yards. It wasn't much better for the other running backs on the roster either. TreVeyon Henderson was rarely used (three carried, nine yards), while Corey Kiner (four carries, 13 yards) appeared to be second-in-command for most of the first half .
"We didn't run the ball well enough, but moved it however we needed to move it, which sometimes you're going to have days like that," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "I though we'd be able to run it a little better. We didn't. ... We'd like to run the ball a little better, but it didn't happen tonight."
Stevenson has been on some really good Patriots teams and some really bad Patriots team. That play, although it didn't spark a comeback on Thursday, could be a sign that there's something below the surface for this year's group that's ready to come out.
"We know this team's gonna fight," he said. "We got some relentless people in this locker room. That's great, that's great. We just gotta come out and win games though, that's the main thing. We just gotta watch the film and see what we did well. We had shots to win the game. Bunch of credit to them, that's a great team. But we had shots to win the game, I think."

title: Patriots Stock Report: Which Position Groups Rose, Fell vs. Bears?
full_text:
The New England Patriots' battle with the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on Thursday night had the visiting team flash plenty of inconsistencies.
Many of New England's positions shined, or struggled, as a collective. Here are the stock reports on the groups which had the biggest impacts in either regard.
New England's wide receiver room may have been the biggest contributor to the team's loss on Thursday night. A.J. Brown, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism and Kyle Williams combined for just seven receptions on 12 targets. Those catches went for 87 yards and no touchdowns.
As the primary target at wide receiver, Brown struggled once again. He has caught just three passes in each of his trio of games as a Patriot.
"I think (the Bears' defense) did a really good job," Brown said after the game. "Early on, (offensive coordinator) Josh (McDaniels) tried to do a really good job of getting me involved and Drake just was taking what they were giving. They were trying to take me away early on, and that's just kind of how the game played."
What the Patriots lacked in production from its wide receivers, it made up for with its tight ends. Veteran Hunter Henry tallied seven receptions for 71 yards, including multiple crucial first down conversions. Also, rookie Eli Raridon got on the board for three receptions, 56 yards and a touchdown.
The main highlight from those two? Raridon's 30-yard score late in the third quarter.
Drake Maye DIME to Eli Raridon 🪙 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/ajUvbcD8Oo
"(He's) great, man," Henry said on Thursday about Raridon. "Just continuing to get better and growing that confidence. A lot of fun to play with."
To address the elephant in the room, yes, Drake Maye's interception was borderline unacceptable. After being turnover-free in his last two games, the third-year signal caller reverted back to his early-season struggles by tossing a pick in the red zone.
Other than that, however, Maye was near-perfect on the evening. He finished 24/31 passing for 321 yards and two touchdowns, alongside the interception. On the ground, he added an extra 26 yards and a score.
In a game where he was constantly pressured, and his receivers were struggling to get open, Maye was one of the lone reasons why New England had any chance of beating Chicago.
"He gave us a chance," Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said about Maye after the loss. "He competed. And I know he'd like to have that throw back to Eli, but I thought that he really competed. Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football, he gave us a chance."
The Patriots' pass defense was borderline non-existent on Thursday. Their completion percentage allowed (66.7%) was largely aided by a few bad drops by Bears receivers. Plus, Caleb Williams tossed for over 300 yards and two touchdowns.
While the defense as a whole improved in the second half, the secondary struggled immensely in the first 30 minutes against dynamic wide receiver Luther Burden III. The second-year pass catcher hauled in four receptions for 130 yards and a touchdown — all coming in the first half of play.
New England's running back room struggled immensely in the ground game, but helped make up for the wide receivers' struggles in the pass game. Rhamondre Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner combined for only 13 carries and 44 yards, and played a significant role in the Patriots' slow start to the night.
However, Stevenson also ended the night with five receptions for a team-high 93 yards and a touchdown. The score came on a 48-yard catch-and-run with no time remaining in the first half to cut the Bears' lead to one possession.
Crazy things happening 🤯 @budlight | 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/QdmQ1DOPPX
Between penalties, pressures allowed on Maye and an inability to find momentum in the run game, the Patriots offensive line combined for a perfectly imperfect performance on Thursday.
Offensive tackle Morgan Moses was called for a hold to back New England up from 2nd-and-2 to 2nd-and-12. Plus, he allowed three pressures and a sack on the evening, per PFF. Every other starter on the line allowed one pressure and was called for a penalty, except for center Jared Wilson who had a clean sheet in both regards.

title: Patriots, Bears QB Duel Lived Up To The Hype
full_text:
CHICAGO — It lived up to the hype, that's for sure.
The second-ever meeting between Drake Maye and Caleb Williams was far better than their first one two seasons ago. The young quarterbacks for the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears had excellent days for their respective sides on Thursday Night Football, with Williams' Bears grabbing the 30-24 win in the final moments .
"Shoulda, woulda, coulda," Maye told reporters postgame. "I'm proud of the guys for the effort. I think we did some good things, we've got a lot of stuff to clean up."
But that loss wasn't on Maye's shoulders, at least not entirely. The 24-year-old went 24-for-31 for 347 total yards and three total touchdowns (two passing, one rushing). It was a fantastic effort by Maye, who kept the Patriots offense in the game all night.
And yet, it was Williams' scrambling and elite arm talent that led the Bears. He finished the night going 22-for-33 for 308 yards and two passing touchdowns, and hit Rome Odunze on a pair of first downs that started to break the Patriots' proverbial defensive back.
It was two juggernauts dueling it out.
"Drake's a competitor, man," tight end Hunter Henry said in the locker room. "That's what he does. We always got a chance when 10's back there, that's for sure."
"He did a great job extending plays," A.J. Brown, who caught three passes in the loss, said. "He did great."
Maye's one blip on his radar was a bad interception in the first half. Looking to hit rookie Eli Raridon in the end zone, he didn't put enough air on his pass and Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson picked it off. It was Maye's third INT thrown in the end zone this season, the most in the entire NFL.
On the other side of the field, Williams completed eight passes of 20+ yards, tied for the most by any quarterback in 2026. He didn't turn the ball over and used his legs to buy some time for his receivers, which hurt the Patriots secondary's ability to defend "the second play."
"We talked about it all week," Christian Gonzalez said. "He's very gifted with how he can run and how he can extend plays. ... You gotta defend the second play. There's a play and then there's a second play with a quarterback like Caleb."
"Anytime a quarterback that's as mobile as him gets out of the pocket, they definitely put stress on the DBs," Charles Woods told Patriots On SI. "It's definitely difficult, but that's what we signed up."
Williams ran for just 18 yards, but his legs helped set up some of the game's biggest plays. He rolled out to find Colston Loveland on a 12-yard touchdown in the third quarter. He escaped the pocket to help pick up big conversions late in the fourth. He was the victor in Week 7, and deservingly so.
If this was the type of matchup these two young quarterbacks can provide , watch out NFL. Instead of rookie gunslingers on bad teams in 2024, these were two grown quarterbacks that offer plenty of skills under center. It was a fun one to watch at Soldier Field.
"I just appreciate we have him back there and (to) be able to block for him," Walter Rouse, who started his first game of the season at left guard, told Patriots On SI. "Drake's an awesome, great guy."
The loss wasn't the outcome the Patriots had hoped for, but it was a gutsy effort by their quarterback. It's just the latest in a string of them, and it's proving why he's the face of this franchise.
"He gave us a chance," Mike Vrabel said. "He competed. ... He'll learn from it like he always does. I'm glad he's ours."

title: Patriots Defense Struggles, and 6 More Takeaways From Groggy TNF Loss to Bears
full_text:
CHICAGO — At some point, the New England Patriots ' three game-winning streak was going to end. That happened at Soldier Field Thursday, as they ran into a Chicago Bears-shaped buzzsaw and couldn't get anything cooking.
Struggles upfront on an injury-depleted offensive line, penalties and an inability to stop the chunk play was what caused the Patriots to drop this one 30-24 to the Bears on a national stage. They kept it close in the final frame, but several long first downs from Rome Odunze wiped that dream away.
Drake Maye (23-for-29, 305 passing yards, two total touchdowns) was efficient, but couldn't will his team to the win. Instead, it was Caleb Williams (22-for-33, 308 passing yards, two passing touchdowns) who emerged victorious, handing the Patriots their first loss in the city of Chicago since 2000.
Here's what happened, and what it means moving forward.
The Patriots lost Alijah Vera-Tucker (who was placed on IR pregame) and Ben Brown last week in their win over the New York Jets. So they had to turn to Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse to step into the starting lineup.
it didn't go that well. The Bears continued to dial up pressure — both up the middle and off the edge — to make life difficult for Maye in the pocket. Chicago really got into the backfield consistently, allowing just 70 yards on the ground. They also sacked Maye twice.
The Patriots would get on the board with a seven-yard rushing touchdown from Maye, but for the most part, the ground game was not the way to go. They consistently lost battles in the trenches and it really took the running attack out of the playbook down the line.
For the entire first half, the Patriots struggled to stay on Burden in coverage. The speedy wideout — who came into the game with just 361 receiving yards on the year — tallied 130 receiving yards with a touchdown.
A 58-yard catch-and-run early helped set up a four-yard D'Andre Swift touchdown in the first quarter, and he'd hit paydirt himself on a weaving 24-yard score. The Patriots would soon adapt, and Burden would be shut down in the second half and held without a catch.
After several weeks of playing nearly-flawless football, Maye made his first bad decision in a while. Driving down the field, he tried to hit Eli Raridon in the end zone in the second quarter. He didn't put enough juice on the throw, and it was picked off by Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson.
That was the third time in seven games that Maye has been intercepted in the end zone this year, the most by any NFL quarterback. Other than that, the Patriots quarterback was good at getting the ball out to his open receivers.
He could have had A.J. Brown deep down the sideline , but the perfectly thrown ball was deflected by Malik Muhammed in coverage. Brown's night ended with just three catches and he's yet to make that big play the Patriots need him to make .
After Burden ran his way in for a touchdown and a 20-7 lead, it looked like the Patriots were heading into the locker room on life support. But somehow, someway, they made something out of nothing.
Maye connected with A.J. Brown on his first reception of the game, good for 18 yards. The Patriots would call a timeout with three ticks left and line up for appeared to be a Hail Mary attempt.
Instead, they checked it down to Rhamondre Stevenson out of the backfield. He would run and pick up some yardage against a Chicago defense playing pretty soft coverage. Then he'd cut back and pick up some more yardage. And more, until the Patriots running back waltzed into the end zone untouched. That 48-yard pickup was the longest play by New England all night, and got them back into the game.
On the Bears' opening drive of the second half, they'd pick up chunk play after chunk play to drive deep into New England territory. Williams would roll out and hit tight end Colston Loveland — who'd power his way into the end zone and give the Bears the 27-14 lead.
But not so fast. Maye and the Patriots go on an impressive drive of their own in response. They drive 80 yards on nine plays, and it ends with Maye hitting Rairdon down the right seam for a 30-yard touchdown.
After back-to-back drives where both offenses sputtered out, the Bears would try to extend their lead with a Cairo Santos field goal. That 53-yard attempt would hit the right upright, giving the Patriots a chance — a chance they'd squander away after giving up a big sack on second down.
All night, the Patriots defense was just getting gashed . Whether it was a long pass from Williams to Odunze or a crisp off-tackle run for Swift that picked up a first down, it was difficult for the Patriots to make life difficult for the home team. The Bears had more than 400 total yards of offense, and that was even converting just four third downs.
But they were oh so close plenty of times. Kevin Byard nearly broke up a pass, but a dart from Williams to Odunze turned into a 21-yard pickup. Neither Milton Williams nor Christian Barmore — the team's top stars on the interior — could muster up any consistent pressure. Williams' ability to move in the pocket and scramble if needed really limited the impact that the Patriots could have done.
Barmore would sack Williams on a third down with 1:39 left, but Santos would drill a 58-field goal one play later to essentially put the nail in the coffin. Barmore would also get banged up on the play and leave the game.
The Patriots lost to the Bears, but they also kept beating themselves.
They were flagged 10 times for 71 total yards, and consistently put themselves behind the 8-ball. A false start from Pryor turned what would have been a fourth down conversion attempt into a punt, and a Cory Durden encroachment flag gave the Bears a first down after the final two-minute warning.
It wasn't just the Patriots, though. The Bears were also called for eight penalties for 56 yards.
The Patriots, after playing two games in five days and now sitting at 4-3, will now have the next three days off.

title: Patriots Week 7 Inactives vs. Bears: Breaking Down What to Expect at OL Tonight
full_text:
CHICAGO — In under 90 minutes, two teams with Super Bowl aspirations will duke it out in front of a national audience. The New England Patriots and Chicago Bears , both sporting 4-2 records, will do battle on Thursday Night Football — but not at full strength.
The Patriots have taken a beating in recent weeks . They've had to put a number of players on injured reserve this season, including wide receiver Romeo Doubs this week. It hasn't been easy sledding for the defending AFC champions, and a short week certainly won't help that.
Here's a look at the inactives from both sides, including key offensive linemen who won't be able to dress:
QB Behren Morton (emergency third QB)
QB Case Keenum (emergency third QB)
RB Kyle Monangai (thumb/toe)
CB Channing Canada (hamstring)
CB Karon Prunty (hamstring)
For the Patriots, there isn't any surprises. Head coach Mike Vrabel shared all of these names (other than Behren Morton and Joshua Farmer) at his final press conference of the week on Wednesday.
Rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover will return to the lineup after being inactive for the last  five games. Behren Morton, who's been the third quarterback all season, won't be able to play unless Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito leave with injuries.
For the Bears, losing their downhill running back in Kyle Monangai is a break for the Patriots — who have struggled against the run in recent weeks. They'll still have to deal with D'Andre Swift , who had two touchdowns on 44 yards a week ago against Atlanta.
"Their runners or anybody that touches the ball is going to be a physical player, is going to be a tough tackle," Vrabel said. "We'll have to be great tacklers."
After Alijah Vera-Tucker and Ben Brown went down a week ago, the Patriots got inspiring outings from their backups. Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor , the last two active linemen on the game day roster, stepped up to fill in at both guard spots. They'll now be in the starting lineup tonight, with Rouse handling the left side and Pryor the right.
It's just another offensive line combination that the Patriots will need to navigate through . They lost Mike Onwenu early in the season, and then lost his backup Greg Van Roten one week later. Just a few games later, and we're seeing two players who didn't spend the summer in New England starting a primetime game. Vera-Tucker was placed on IR prior to kickoff , ruling him out for the next four games.
Vrabel was asked Wednesday about the possibility of rookie tackle Caleb Lomu, who's gotten reps on both sides of the line the last two weeks, potentially kicking inside at guard.
"We have a lot of consideration," he said. "We go through things, different scenarios. We're going to go with where we finished on Sunday and see what that looks like, and then have everybody else ready to go."
The Patriots are also down three cornerbacks, the biggest name being Carlton Davis. He's been dealing with a neck injury for a lot of the season, and this will be his fourth missed game of the year. They're also down rookies Channing Canada and Karon Prunty, who both have hamstring injuries.
Davis is the team's second-best cornerback and easily their top one when it comes to playing the run. But he's struggled to stay healthy in 2026, and while he was spotted at practice for the first time in three weeks leading up to this game, the Patriots still didn't feel comfortable rolling him out there.
The Patriots will have four active cornerbacks for this matchup against a high-flying Bears offense, with Christian Gonzalez, Marcus Jones, Charles Woods and Kindle Vildor ready to go. Second-year safety Elliott Davison has also gotten snaps at cornerback this season in a reserve role.
The Patriots nearly got a scare at cornerback, as Gonzalez was downgraded to questionable pregame with an illness. However, he was warming up on the field and will suit up.
The Bears come into this matchup with one of the league's best defenses — especially against the run. But they rank 14th in the NFL in passing defense through six games, and with a few players banged up in the secondary, the Patriots can try to push the ball through the air.
Chicago will be without cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, who was ruled out with a hip injury. They'll also line up without Nick McCloud (who's played in just two games this year) on the field. They do have Kyler Gordon back, who played last week after opening the year on the PUP list, but he's still trying to knock the rust off.
If the Patriots want to try and air the ball out against a secondary that isn't at full strength, they could end up putting up a bunch of points in a hurry. Avoiding a stout Bears run defense, especially early in drives, could be beneficial.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly: Saints Finally Win, but Major Problems Remain
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints finally have a reason to celebrate. Their 34-27 victory over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Sunday was far from seamless, but it brought a much-needed end to a troublesome stretch.
Riding a three-game losing streak and facing mounting questions about the franchise's direction, New Orleans desperately needed a win. The Saints delivered by overcoming an early 10-0 deficit, though they nearly squandered a commanding 24-point lead late in the second half.
Quarterback Tyler Shough completed 16 of 30 passes for 144 yards and three touchdowns, guiding an offense that showed encouraging progress on the ground. Meanwhile, the defense created three interceptions despite struggling to contain New York's passing game.
The win gives head coach Kellen Moore 's squad welcome breathing room, after the team entered the week under heavy scrutiny following critical remarks from franchise icon Drew Brees and owner Gayle Benson .
Still, the team's inability to comfortably close out the game after building a 34-10 advantage underscores ongoing concerns about their consistency and ability to finish strong.
Here is a look at the good, bad and ugly from the Saints' victory over the Giants.
Following weeks of criticism regarding a stagnant ground attack, the Saints may have uncovered a workable formula.
New Orleans ran for a season-high 175 yards, offering vital balance to an offense that had relied far too heavily on Tyler Shough to make plays.
Kendre Miller paced the backfield with 70 yards on 20 carries, while C.J. Donaldson added 39 yards on six attempts. Alvin Kamara chipped in 34 yards on seven carries, and Shough contributed 32 yards along with a rushing touchdown.
This collective output was an encouraging sign for a unit that had failed to establish any momentum during its three-game slide.
However, the Saints still have considerable work ahead.
Even so, efficiency remains an issue; Miller averaged just 3.5 yards per carry, reflecting the play-to-play inconsistency that still lingers.
Lineman Jeremiah Wright provided a notable spark after replacing the injured Cesar Ruiz at right guard. His presence was felt in the second half, as the Saints repeatedly—and successfully—ran behind the right side of the line.
To sustain this progress, the offensive line must open cleaner lanes up front rather than depending on backfield effort to gain positive yardage.
While far from dominant, Sunday's performance marked a meaningful step toward a more balanced attack.
Despite forcing three interceptions, the Saints' defensive backfield repeatedly yielded big plays during New York's late comeback bid.
Receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely caused major problems throughout the contest.
Nabers hauled in 12 receptions for 165 yards, while Likely added six catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.
After replacing starter Jameis Winston , backup J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards in just over 11 minutes, orchestrating three straight touchdown drives to cut a 34-10 deficit to seven points.
New Orleans did deliver key playmaking moments: Martin Emerson Jr. picked off two passes, Julian Blackmon intercepted another, and the pass rush brought down Winston four times.
However, surrendering 461 total yards (377 passing) highlights persistent pass-coverage issues that defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must resolve.
For three quarters, the Saints looked poised for their most convincing win of the year—a strong statement following three straight home defeats.
Instead, they nearly suffered a catastrophic fourth-quarter collapse.
After trailing 10-0 early, New Orleans reeled off 34 unanswered points using balanced rushing, opportunistic turnovers, and efficient red-zone execution.
Shough's 18-yard touchdown strike to Chris Olave early in the fourth quarter pushed the lead to 34-10, prompting the Saints to begin rotating in reserves.
However, the momentum quickly shifted.
With McCarthy at quarterback, New York scored 17 unanswered points over the final 11 minutes, exploiting defensive breakdowns and stalling offensive possessions.
An offense that had scored on four straight drives suddenly went cold, finishing an alarming 4-for-15 on third down.
Meanwhile, the defense surrendered multiple scoring drives as New York steadily chipped away at the deficit.
The Giants eventually cut the lead to 34-27 and drove deep into New Orleans territory. The Saints survived only when McCarthy's fourth-down pass to Likely fell incomplete near the end zone.
For a Saints team already facing criticism over its lack of consistency, nearly blowing a 24-point advantage raises legitimate questions about its ability to finish games.
Moore and his staff deserve credit for halting the losing streak, but nearly letting a 24-point lead slip away shows that New Orleans still has significant work ahead to compete with top-tier opponents.

The sequence completely changed the momentum.

Although Stalbird's contribution won't receive the same attention as Shough's four-touchdown performance or Martin Emerson Jr. 's two interceptions, his forced fumble was arguably the game's most important play.
After weeks of heavy criticism in regard to its horrendous rushing attack, the Saints may have figured out the formula.

Miller averaged just 3.5 yards a carry, highlighting the inconsistency that continues to plague the rushing attack despite the improved overall numbers.

The Saints need their offensive front, including Wright when he is involved, to create more consistent running lanes rather than relying on individual efforts to generate positive yardage.
Sunday's performance was hardly a dominant rushing effort, but it represented a meaningful step forward for an offense desperately searching for balance.
Despite grabbing three interceptions, the Saints' secondary once struggled once again against a solid receiving corps in coverage during New York's fourth-quarter comeback.
Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely torched New Orleans’ secondary all game.
Nabers recorded 12 catches for 165 yards, while Likely had six catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.
After replacing Jameis Winston, J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards in just over 11 minutes, sparking three straight touchdown drives to trim a 34-10 deficit to seven points.
Still, the defense created crucial takeaways: Martin Emerson Jr. had two interceptions (one off McCarthy), Julian Blackmon picked off Winston, and the pass rush logged four sacks on Winston.
Yet, allowing 461 total yards (377 passing) highlights the already serious concerns on whether or not the secondary can slow so. Defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must fix these coverage breakdowns to prevent future collapses.
Few teams entered Week 6 under more pressure than the Saints.
Following three consecutive losses, including a disappointing 23-13 defeat against the Minnesota Vikings , New Orleans found itself under intense scrutiny from fans, former players and ownership.
Former Saints quarterback Drew Brees, who called the game for Fox and was inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor at halftime during the loss to the Vikings, criticized the team's offense and Moore's play-calling .
A few days later, Saints owner Gayle Benson publicly expressed her frustration with the team's 1-4 start during a speaking engagement at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club, making it clear that recent performances were unacceptable.
Benson specifically challenged the team's leadership, including Moore and general manager Mickey Loomis , to address the mistakes that had contributed to the disappointing start.
Those comments placed additional pressure on Moore, whose second season as head coach has been defined by inconsistent performances and questions about the team's direction.
Sunday's victory provided a much-needed response.
The Saints showed resilience after falling behind 10-0, capitalized on turnovers and demonstrated the offensive explosiveness that had been largely absent during their losing streak.
More importantly, they found a way to win.
Yet blowing nearly all of a 24-point fourth-quarter lead highlighted the issues behind Benson's criticism. With execution and closing troubles nearly turning a blowout into a loss, the 2-4 Saints face major questions before playing the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris. Snapping the streak offers short-term relief, but New Orleans must show real growth to make this a true turning point.

title: How to Watch Giants vs. Texans: Time, TV, Radio and Referee for Week 7
full_text:
Ever since two-time Super Bowl MVP quarterback Eli Manning retired after a 16-year run with the organization, the New York Giants and their fans have had to come to grips with how spoiled they were to witness rare consistency at the sport’s most important position.
Manning finally hung up his cleats after the 2019 season, but even before that decision, the Giants had started testing the waters with other gunslingers around him. Since then, 12 different players have suited up to lead Big Blue and largely failed to live up to his legacy.
Those include Jaxson Dart, who the franchise believes is its long-term answer but who has run into injury problems, including a season-ending knee injury in Week 2, and his initial backup, Jameis Winston, who has assumed the role in the team’s previous four contests.
With head coach John Harbaugh electing to make a change at quarterback ahead of Week 7, J.J. McCarthy becomes the 13th man on the short list, and his first task at the helm won’t be an easy one as the Giants travel to Houston to face the Texans on Sunday.
The Texans’ 2-4 record might not be the shiniest in the league, but they have a few solid pieces that will test McCarthy and the Giants’ roster. Quarterback C.J. Stroud has started to heat up just in time for the Texans to get back one of their key offensive weapons in Tank Dell, who will line up wide opposite another All-Pro threat in Nico Collins.
On the defensive side of the field, Houston boasts what some might argue are the two best pass rushers in football. Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter are among the most productive duos in the league with 14 sacks and 60 pressures between them in six games, both stats to be feared by a Giants offensive line that has struggled under the weight of injuries.
The Texans’ two advantages have the football public leaning heavily toward the host team and doubting McCarthy, who has started only 10 games since being drafted No. 10 overall in 2024 and has gone through ebbs and flows in Minnesota.
For Harbaugh’s Giants, however, the switch to the former national championship signal-caller has created nothing but confidence throughout the locker room, especially on offense, where McCarthy’s strong arm and capable legs could reopen the full playbook once designed for Dart.
It’s certainly a big spot for McCarthy to prove himself once again. The Giants remain at the top of a very underperforming NFC East, where the three teams below have been crumbling in recent weeks, leaving the door wide open for them to chase a division title with a few more bold wins in the second half of the season.
Coming off a poor team performance against the New Orleans Saints, in which McCarthy entered the lopsided affair in the fourth quarter and nearly brought the Giants back from their  deficit, he has no better opportunity to help New York achieve that goal and change the image of his career.
The Giants got all they could squeeze out of the “Jameis Winston experience,” and the veteran deserves kudos for leading the organization into a 3-2-1 start that keeps them relevant in the postseason discussion.
After watching a few wild yet sharply executed drives by McCarthy at the end of a game that should have been an ugly blowout, Harbaugh and the Giants see there is another level they might be able to tap into with the third-year quarterback.
It’s time for the J.J. McCarthy experience for a full 60 minutes in Houston, where the Giants hope to escape with a much-needed win before their bye week.
Check in with New York Giants On SI for all the pregame, in-game, and postgame coverage.
Sunday will mark the seventh regular-season meeting between the Giants and Texans since the series began in 2002. New York leads the series 5-1.
The Texans captured the first game on Nov. 24, 2002, with a close 16-14 win over the Giants. Since then, Big Blue has dominated the series, winning the next five games, including the most recent in 2022, when it leveled Houston 24-16.
Most games have been tight, with only two separated by more than 10 points.
The game will air on FOX. For the second straight week, Adam Amin will call the game, former NFL quarterback Drew Brees will be the analyst, and Kristina Pink will report from the sidelines.
Giants fans can listen to the game on WFAN 101.9 FM. Bob Papa will handle play-by-play, joined by Giants legend Carl Banks as the analyst and Howard Cross as the sideline reporter.
Land Clark will be the lead referee for Sunday’s contest. Clark has been officiating in the NFL since 2018 and was promoted to referee in 2020. He also has college experience officiating Pac-12 games.

title: Giants’ Run Defense Is a Problem, but D.J. Reader Is Not
full_text:
Through the first six weeks of the 2026 season, the New York Giants ’ run defense has once again been a glaring problem that has hurt the team’s overall performance.
Following their crushing 34-27 Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, in which they allowed 175 rushing yards- the third time this season they have given up at least 163, questions have been rising as to whether the organization did enough to fix the defense’s biggest weakness, which ranked last in yards per carry last season.
Those concerns intensified in the offseason, when the Giants sent shockwaves by trading two-time All-Pro defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence to the Cincinnati Bengals.
The move shipped off a disgruntled star but left a gaping hole at one of the game’s most important positions.
With the money freed up by the deal, they signed two proven veterans, D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris, to man the middle of the defensive front.
Both have been promising, but it has been painfully obvious that the depth behind them isn’t holding up for Dennard Wilson’s group whenever either exits the field.
As New York heads into Week 7 with the league’s second-worst run defense , it has to find a way to strengthen its run response and give the pass rush and secondary more chances to dominate, as they did in the impressive wins in Weeks 3 and 4.
For now, the Giants can at least hang their hats on a workable foundation in the trenches with Reader, who is outpacing his talented predecessor.
Even with Lawrence’s decline in production amid injuries, which sparked a contract stalemate and his eventual trade, the Giants knew they wouldn’t easily replace a player of his caliber.
Not long ago, Lawrence was in the discussion as the NFL’s best defensive tackle, coming off a career-high 2024 season in which he had 9.5 sacks, 21 tackles (25 stops) and the second-highest run-defense grade among players at his position.
An untimely elbow injury cost Lawrence the final five games of that season. When he returned in 2025, both his production and his overall effort came into question as he finished the year with his lowest grade in five seasons and no sacks despite playing a full 17-game slate.
Even so, the move drew criticism of the Giants for shipping off arguably the best player on their roster, who had grown frustrated with the constant losing that engulfed the franchise for most of his tenure and led to the hiring of John Harbaugh.
In addition, some questioned the transition to Reader, the 32-year-old veteran whose recent stats suggested he might be past his prime and thus no more than a temporary rental for Big Blue.
Through six games with the Giants, Reader has been the lone bright spot on the team’s defensive front and, compared with Lawrence in Cincinnati, has proven himself the more productive player.
Reader got off to a slow start as a gap stuffer, posting no more than three tackles along the line of scrimmage in his first five games. His peak outing came against the Saints’ 30th-ranked rushing attack, when he logged a season-high seven run stops with no missed tackles.
With those numbers, Reader leads the Giants’ defense with an 85.3 run-defense grade. Among interior defenders with at least 100 run-defense snaps, he ranks in the top three in tackles (16), stops (14) and average depth of tackle (2.3 yards), while committing no penalties.
Lawrence has had a more impressive start with the Bengals as a pass rusher, generating 19 pressures, including three sacks and three hits. Against the run, he trails Reader with only 10 tackles, 12 stops and a missed-tackle rate of 14.3%.
It’s worth noting that Reader has been a two-down player throughout his career, compared with Lawrence, whose size made him an every-down weapon.
Reader has also commanded significant attention, holding the league’s highest double-team rate (71.7%) in 2025, which boosted his value on the free-agent market, where New York won the bid for his services.
It is still premature to crown the Giants the winners of the blockbuster deal that landed them the No. 10 pick used to select Francis Mauigoa and fortify their starting offensive line. The early returns suggest they have at least found the right replacement for Lawrence to build the rest of their defensive front around.
Building out that front will be one of the team’s looming offseason priorities, as some of its younger pieces need to develop into larger roles. Harbaugh also wants physicality at the line of scrimmage to be one of his team’s tenets.

title: Three Key Matchups the Giants Must Win to Upset the Texans
full_text:
After two weeks of mixed offensive performances and disappointing results, John Harbaugh and the New York Giants are switching things up at quarterback, with J.J. McCarthy taking over for Jameis Winston ahead of a pivotal matchup with the Houston Texans.
The Giants are hoping McCarthy’s presence will spark an offense that lost some of its luster when Jaxson Dart went down and became too one-dimensional in its previous two games against the Washington Commanders and New Orleans Saints, behind Winston’s inconsistent decision-making and an unestablished running game.
That said, New York will need more than its new starter’s efforts to leave Houston with a huge win. Here are the three key matchups the Giants must dominate to stun the Texans and improve to 4-2-1 before their bye week.
The Giants are constantly reminded of just how important their two starting offensive tackles, Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor, are to the offense functioning at its highest potential.
For the first time this season, Big Blue faced the Saints’ defense in Week 6 without its stalwart bookends playing every snap. Eluemunor missed the game with a calf injury he sustained against Washington.
Thomas opened on the left side despite a lingering groin ailment, then left in the fourth quarter after the NFL’s medical spotter pulled him for a concussion evaluation.
Without either veteran on the field, the Giants offense faced much more pressure from the New Orleans front, which tallied nine total pressures in the 34-27 loss. Those numbers might pale in comparison to what the Texans’ pass rush could deliver with its dynamic duo of Anderson and Danielle Hunter.
Per the team’s injury report following Friday’s practice, Thomas had no game status and appears to be a full go despite his ongoing groin injury.
Eluemunor, who leads all offensive tackles with a 96.7% pass-block win rate (min. 150 snaps), was listed as questionable, though Harbaugh seemed optimistic he could suit up and play.
The Texans typically flip Anderson, who leads the NFL with 7.5 sacks and holds a 14.1% win rate in his 208 pass-rushing snaps this season, to either side of the formation.
Anderson is a super-talented bull rusher with the power to drive opposing offensive linemen backward into the quarterback and blow up the play before receivers can progress through their routes.
The 6-foot-3, 243-pound defensive end has torn up his immediate matchups in recent weeks, collecting two or more sacks three times and five or more pressures in four of the Texans’ last five games. He can also crash interior gaps quickly, leading to 21 run stops in six starts.
That could pose a problem for either tackle (if they do indeed play) and for anyone who can’t anchor against Anderson’s bull rush.
The Giants are hoping to give McCarthy enough time to operate in the pocket and run extended RPO plays with his dual-threat skill set. If Thomas can’t perform up to par against Anderson, they could have to resort to quick throws instead of betting on a few chunk plays with the quarterback’s impressive arm.
One of the most enjoyable storylines from the Giants’ first six games has been the obvious turnaround in cornerback Deonte Banks’ performance since Dennard Wilson took over the defense.
Banks, a lame-duck starter since the Giants declined his fifth-year rookie option in May, has largely quieted the fan base’s complaints about his coverage with a much-improved 50% opponent catch rate allowed. He is tied with Greg Newsome II for the most pass deflections in the secondary (4).
Some old shades of Banks’ miscues have reared their ugly heads in recent weeks. He has drawn a penalty in three straight games and has allowed completions on 60% or more of targets against him since Week 4.
That includes last Sunday against Chris Olave and the Saints, when the former first-round pick out of Maryland allowed three catches on five targets for 36 yards, with a long of 18 yards, and fell asleep, letting Olave cash in one grab for a touchdown in the Saints’ win.
One week later, Banks’ newest assignment will be a much tougher one as he braces to slow down Texans wide receiver Nico Collins, who has wreaked havoc on opposing secondaries. Houston’s defense, meanwhile, is banged up.
Collins has been one of the most productive pass-catchers this season, averaging a team-high 80.8 yards per contest with a 78.6% catch rate , third-best among receivers with at least 25 targets.
The 6-foot-4, 222-pound Collins hasn’t been much of a deep-threat weapon for Houston’s offense, but he’s been efficient against press coverage, a staple of Wilson’s system. He has hauled in 83.3% of his targets against man coverage, including a perfect 2-for-2 on contested catches.
Banks has shown some strong flashes as an aggressive ballhawk and has helped the Giants flip the endings of a couple of games by getting his hands in front of the pass.
He’ll need to do a lot better against a craftier receiver like Collins, who might try to counteract the peskier coverage by drawing costly penalties against Banks.
That is the last thing his team needs when facing a Texans offense that ranks 15th in third-down conversions and will look to pile on points to pressure McCarthy and the Giants offense.
If Banks can shut Collins down, Houston can’t rely on its ground game to carry the load, as it sits in the bottom third of the league in both attempts and yards.
Giants receiver Malik Nabers promised to get open for his new starting quarterback against the Texans, but that might not be as easy if he has to spar with Derek Stingley Jr.
Nabers has found his groove after a long, grueling ACL rehab that began in Week 5 of last season, and he showed flashes of the dominant pass catcher he can be with three straight 100-plus-yard receiving outings.
Since Week 5, the 23-year-old Nabers has racked up 23 catches for 286 yards and a touchdown, despite Winston's errant throws.
The Giants star really exploded once McCarthy took over in the fourth quarter against the Saints, posting a season-high 12 catches for 165 yards and his fourth game with at least one contested catch.
Given the Giants’ unimpressive receiving depth and sputtering run game, Nabers will likely need to be a major factor in moving the ball through the air and attacking the Texans’ defense, which wants to stunt his confidence with its relentless pass rush.
Nabers’ speed and hands could be a huge asset if the Giants need to prioritize short throws and low crossing routes to counteract the blitz. It wouldn’t be surprising if the Texans call upon Stingley to be their own aggressive cornerback who frustrates the opponent’s top target.
Since 2024, Stingley has been one of the NFL’s stingiest perimeter defenders, allowing an average 52% completion rate in that span.
He excels at getting his hands on the football and cutting off direct throws that could become forced turnovers, leading to interceptions and 23 pass deflections. As bold as McCarthy can be with his decisive throws, he’ll need to be extra careful about ball placement to avoid Stingley bruising his stat sheet with turnovers.
Stingley will also make it tough for Nabers or any other receiver to gain extra yards after the catch, given his strong run-stopping play and fewer than 10 missed tackles in four of his first five seasons.
The Texans could even call on him as a pressure guy in select packages or have him crash the line of scrimmage to stop the run game they’re hoping to revive this week.
All that said, most of the Giants’ passing production has come through the heroics of Nabers and Isaiah Likely. McCarthy will look for his guys, and they’re vowing to be reliable.
Nabers’ reliability will depend on finding ways to beat Stingley off the snap and create separation that pushes the ball toward the end zone, where they’ll need to score to keep up with Houston’s fiery offense.

title: Giants Draw Land Clark’s Officiating Crew for Week 7 Game Against Texans. A Scouting Report
full_text:
Over six weeks, the New York Giants have been penalized 46 times for 374 yards, putting them 13th in the league .
Three times this season (Weeks 1, 3 and 6), the Giants have drawn 10 penalties, though the last two times they drew that many, the yardage didn’t top 100 yards as it did in Week 1, when they racked up 114 yards.
This week, the Giants are facing Land Clark’s crew in Houston. Clark and company have issued 95 penalties (the sixth-most among officiating crews this season), of which 80 have been accepted for 638 yards through six games.
Clark is a graduate of the league’s NFL Officiating Development program and previously worked as a referee in the Pac-12.
He initially entered the NFL as a field judge in 2018 and was promoted to referee two seasons later after longtime NFL referee Walt Anderson retired.
The Giants drew Clark twice last season. During a Week 3 loss versus the Kansas City Chiefs (Russell Wilson’s final start for the franchise), they accrued seven penalties for 82 yards.
When the squad beat the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 17, it was assessed eight penalties for 58 yards.
Clark’s crew underwent a shakeup this past offseason, with five new members assigned to work with him.
They include down judge Dale Keller, previously with Bill Vinovich’s crew; line judge Stephen Ray, who joins the NFL officials after having worked in the SEC; side judge Dave Hawkshaw, previously with Clay Martin’s crew; replay official Gavin Anderson, previously with Craig Wrolstad’s crew; and replay assistant Mark Evans, who comes to the NFL from the Mountain West division of college football.
Hawkshaw, an eight-year official, previously served as a side judge, so this year marks a position assignment change for him.
Umpire Mark Pellis, field judge Jabir Walker and back judge Brad Freeman are the only returning members of Clark’s crew from last year. All three have at least 10 years of NFL officiating experience.
The Giants (3-2-1) and Texans (2-4) get underway Sunday at Reliant Stadium. Kickoff is set for 1:05 p.m. ET.

title: Giants Activate Paulson Adebo, Place Tremaine Edmunds on IR Ahead of Texans Game
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ roster churn continued Saturday as the team activated cornerback Paulson Adebo from injured reserve. It placed inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds on IR with a season-ending shoulder injury.
Adebo, who was placed on IR at the start of the season with a knee injury, will get the start at cornerback with Greg Newsome II (concussion) declared out this week.
“He’s a legit corner. He’s a cover corner, he tackles. He’s been a high-end corner in this league. I think he’s really determined to play that way,” head coach John Harbaugh said of Adebo and what the cornerback can bring to the defense.
“I think he’s finally probably healthy and ready to go. I can’t wait to see it.”
Adebo is in the middle of a three-year, $54 million contract with the Giants that included $38.5 million guaranteed and $34.75 million fully guaranteed.
However, he lost his starting job this summer to Deonte Banks, who, along with Newsome, has been the starting cornerback tandem for the Giants.
The Giants downgraded two players who originally had questionable designations, tight end Theo Johnson (neck) and safety Jevon Holland (concussion).
Johnson did not make the trip with the team to Houston. Holland is believed to have traveled with the team, but it doesn't matter as he's been declared out for Sunday.
In other roster news, receiver Jalin Hyatt, who has been sitting on the team’s practice squad this season, is one of two standard practice squad elevations this week.
Hyatt was the team’s third-round pick in 2023. He has appeared in 41 games with 10 starts over three seasons and has 36 receptions for 470 yards and no touchdowns.
The Giants have only been carrying four receivers of late and last week they nearly lost one when Darnell Mooney suffered an injury that cut into his playing time.
New York also elevated safety Raheem Layne from the practice squad to give them added depth what with Tyler Nubin (neck) having a questionable designation and Holland having been downgraded to out.
